paragraphs: Lycoming County's data center fight is in Muncy Township, a community of just over 1,000 people on the West Branch of the Susquehanna River, and so far it has been fought mostly over paperwork. DANKO Holdings II and Fishlips LLC have applied to build the Muncy Data Center: three buildings totaling about 699,574 square feet, with water storage tanks and a treatment facility, off John Brady Drive near Yetter Road, on about 100 acres of former Muncy Farms cornfields. DANKO is owned by Williamsport developer Dan Klingerman; no power figure, water figure or end user has been made public.

At a special meeting on April 28, 2026, supervisors passed a nine-month moratorium on data centers while the township wrote rules for them; asked whether an application had come in, supervisor Terri Lauchle said no. The Williamsport Sun-Gazette later found a zoning permit application dated April 15 already in the township office, with more filings on April 22 and 27; the township's solicitor, Joe Orso, said the developer read the moratorium agenda and rushed to file before the vote. Orso also says DANKO skipped the normal step of asking the zoning officer for a determination, instead filing a curative amendment arguing the zoning code is invalid because it says nothing about data centers.

Because the township held no hearing within the 60 days state law allows, the developer published a notice in July claiming deemed approval. Neighbors Sean Tetreault and Rae-Ellah Biddle, whose farmhouse sits between Muncy Farms and the site, filed a land use appeal in Lycoming County court in September, arguing the project threatens "unmitigated industrial noise, extreme electrical grid loads, and massive cooling-water consumption" and asking a judge to overturn the deemed approval or send it back for full hearings. Orso has warned the litigation could mean a one- to two-year delay. The township's planning commission is drafting its own data center ordinance, with a public hearing tentatively set for November 4 and adoption tentatively on December 9.

Keel Infrastructure, the bitcoin miner formerly known as Stronghold Digital Mining, wants to add an AI data center campus to its Scrubgrass power plant near Kennerdell, on the Allegheny River. The company says the roughly 650-acre site could eventually support up to 1,363 megawatts of power, though only 63 megawatts is available today and no formal plan has been filed with Venango County. Scrubgrass Township passed a 25-page data center ordinance in July 2026, and county officials say no application has arrived for them to review either.

About 40 residents packed a county planning meeting in June 2026 to raise concerns about power costs, water use and noise, even though officials said nothing had been submitted yet. Commissioner Tim Heffernan put the odds of the data center being built at under 20%, which did not satisfy Rockland attorney Mallory Piercy: "To be told that there is less than a 20% chance of the data center being built is not good enough." The plant also faces an unrelated deadline: a pile of coal ash beside the river must be removed by September 2026 under a settlement with state regulators.

Keel held public information sessions in Clintonville on September 22 and 23, 2026. The company's other Pennsylvania sites, at Panther Creek in Carbon County and Sharon in Mercer County, are further along, with zoning already secured. No tenant or partner for Scrubgrass has been named.

PNK Group, a New York developer, wants to convert a vacant warehouse at 198 Enterprise Blvd. in the Great Stream Commons industrial park outside Allenwood into a data center campus of about 1 million square feet in three buildings, drawing more than 300 megawatts of power. Because Gregg Township's zoning does not list data centers as a use, PNK needs a curative amendment and conditional use approval, and the three supervisors have 45 days from the close of hearings on September 14 to decide. Township solicitor Rick Shoch said the decision will likely come at a special meeting before October 29 at the Warrior Run social hall.

The fight has been over noise. More than 180 people attended the first hearing on July 20, where residents accused company representatives of lying and questioned chief development officer Anton Voronkin about his Russian heritage. PNK says its closed-loop cooling will use only domestic amounts of water and that equipment 770 feet from the nearest property will run at 45 to 48 decibels by day, under the township's 55-decibel limit. At the second hearing, PNK's acoustics witness acknowledged no equipment had actually been chosen yet. "You need to be responsible, physically and financially responsible for that," said Emory Martin of Allenwood.

The opposition has borrowed tactics, including its red shirts, from a successful fight over Talen Energy's data center plan near Montour County's power station. An earlier attempt to build in the same industrial park, by Data Centric LLC, collapsed in 2025 when the company walked away during its due-diligence period, keeping its deposit. In August, supervisors separately approved a land development plan for a substation to serve the warehouse, which officials stressed did not authorize a data center.

Mercer County's first large data center is planned on the site of an old Westinghouse Electric plant in Sharon, and it has moved through local approvals with little opposition. Keel Infrastructure, the New York company known as Bitfarms until 2026, bought the Clark Street property in October 2025 and ran a bitcoin mining operation there until shutting it down on June 29, 2026 ahead of converting to AI. It plans an AI data center of about 110 megawatts on 17 to 18 acres behind the former factory, with two 80-megawatt substations due by the end of 2026. "It's by far the largest investment in Sharon's history," chief operating officer Liam Wilson told the Sharon Herald.

The company has given different investment figures at different meetings: about $1.5 billion at an early April 2026 session in Hermitage, and $4 billion to $5 billion a week later in Sharon. Keel says it will hire 134 full-time staff for at least 20 years, about 40 of them from Sharon, with pay starting above $60,000, plus about 1,300 construction jobs. City Manager Bob Fiscus cited about $7 million in tax revenue from the project. "It seems like a win for us," he said.

Residents asked about power, water and noise. Keel says closed-loop cooling will hold water use under 1,000 gallons a day and it will spend $40 million upgrading power systems, though Wilson could not promise anything about residents' own electric bills. The Sharon Herald's editorial board noted that a much smaller 16-megawatt warehouse project nearby had already been delayed about 30 months by FirstEnergy for power capacity. Sharon's zoning board approved the project in late April with a 70-decibel noise limit and a ban on drawing water from the river, and the city council approved final land development plans on July 15.

Mercer County adopted new countywide data center rules in July, covering noise, water, cooling, emergency planning and decommissioning, though the Sharon project is grandfathered out of them. "If you want to come to Mercer County, we do want to remain rural," said planning director Doniele Russell. Keel has said it will start building and hiring before the end of 2026 and hopes to begin operating in late 2027. Sharon City Council held a special meeting on August 19, 2026 on a new citywide data center zoning ordinance; no result has been published.

Pennsylvania Data Center Partners, working through a subsidiary called Lewistown Development LLC, wants to build a six-building, 1.54 million-square-foot data center complex on about 245.5 acres of farmland in Granville Township, near Lewistown, off Loop Road. The company has not said how much power it would draw. Granville's zoning officer returned the application as incomplete in July for lacking a traffic study certification, and the developer has appealed; the Granville Township Zoning Hearing Board hears that appeal at 7 p.m. on October 1 at the township building on Helen Street, and a related hearing before Judge Aaron Gingrich at the county courthouse follows on October 9.

The township's board fell apart as the fight dragged on. Vice chairman Joseph Fiore Jr. resigned in August and chairman William Page resigned September 17, leaving Terry Stewart as the only supervisor and no quorum to hold meetings or vote on the application. A Mifflin County Court of Common Pleas hearing was scheduled for September 23, 2026 to appoint two interim supervisors; no result has been published. Residents have pushed back over well water, noise and power bills. "I was born here. I've lived here most of my life. But who could listen to that?" resident Corri Hockenberry told local station WHP, adding she would move if the project is built.

Mifflin County commissioners adopted their own data center rules for the county subdivision ordinance in August, separate from the township fight. "We believe we have a very defensible amendment," county planning director Jim Lettiere said.

Monroe County, in the Poconos, has spent 2026 writing data center rules faster than developers have filed data center plans, and the one project with a formal application may escape those rules anyway. It is on Route 209 near East Stroudsburg, in Smithfield Township, on part of Smithfield Gateway, a mixed-use development once meant for restaurants and apartments. Developer DEPG Mosier Associates LP and DEPG of Shawnee II LP first showed a sketch plan in February for two data center buildings of about 125,000 square feet each; the plan was later combined into one two-story, 250,000-square-foot building. No power or water figure has been made public.

Township chairman Jacob Pride was doubtful from the start, saying the switch from a planned live-work-play development to data centers "does not align" with the township's economic development plans. An online petition against the project passed 800 signatures by March, citing deforestation, noise and light pollution. In April the developer filed a conditional use application, a request to be allowed to build because the project meets the zoning ordinance's standards, decided after a public hearing. As of September 22 that hearing had not been scheduled; the township said it was looking for a larger venue for the expected crowd.

The township has since tightened its rules for future projects. On August 12 supervisors approved Ordinance No. 268, which bars data centers from the industrial and economic-development zones and requires conditional use approval, an energy plan, noise limits and a bond for future proposals in a new heavy industrial zone. But officials say the Gateway application, filed before the ordinance passed, will likely be judged under the old rules. Solicitor Ronold Karasek warned the new ordinance could be challenged as exclusionary zoning, a claim that a town's rules are illegally designed to keep a use out entirely.

Perry County's data center proposal sits on land that was meant to be a warehouse hub. MRP Industrial, an East Coast developer of business parks and logistics buildings, dropped a logistics project called Susquehanna Crossings on a 288-acre parcel in Watts Township near Duncannon in late 2025, then submitted a site plan for ten data center buildings of 138,000 square feet each instead. MRP has not said how much power the campus would need or who would use it. Watts Township has no data center rules yet, and is considering a zoning amendment that would allow them.

More than 125 people packed the Watts-Buffalo Community Center for an April 1, 2026 supervisors' meeting, so many it moved outside, and supervisors put off a full hearing. Susan Fulmer, who moved to the township in 2020 to build a retirement home, listed her fears as property values, electricity bills, noise and light pollution, and pollution of the Susquehanna River: "Now it seems like everything we spent our entire lives working for to achieve is going to be taken." The politics do not split along the usual lines: some conservative speakers opposed the project over rising costs, while the county Republican Party chair, Donald McClure, said he supports data centers and was jeered for it. MRP vice president Nate Chadsey told the meeting the site had "significant visual buffering and distance from residents" and would create jobs.

The township held a public hearing on the zoning amendment on June 25, 2026, with a special meeting immediately after to consider adopting it. The outcome has not been made public since. The township's next supervisors' meeting was moved to September 21, 2026.

Greene County's one data center proposal, Project Hummingbird, would cover 1,400 acres of the former Robena coal mine along the Monongahela River in Monongahela Township, next to the small village of Alicia. The developer, International Electric Power of Pittsburgh, plans two natural gas turbines generating 910 megawatts of power on site, plus a battery system and a water treatment plant built by Essential Utilities. The county planning commission voted 8-1 on December 17, 2025, to approve the project's first phase: grading and reclaiming 309 acres and preparing the site for the turbines and water plant.

No tenant has signed on yet. IEP's chief executive, Peter Dailey, said in October 2025 the company was talking with seven potential customers and hoped to sign one by early 2026; by January 2026, according to Farm and Dairy, none had been found. IEP has said it expects to invest $2 billion in the power plant, with the data center itself costing around $10 billion, and estimates 1,500 construction jobs over six years plus 40 to 50 permanent jobs at the plant.

The few families still living in Alicia are divided. "At least when the coal mine was there, it produced something," resident Tom Barton told the county planning commission. "But this just takes water, just takes." Others see it differently: "It might only be 250 jobs, it might be 100 jobs, but it's jobs," said Joseph Martinak of Waynesburg. Dailey has promised noise no louder than about 55 decibels at the property line.
The turbines and data center buildings still need separate approval, and IEP has not said when it expects to seek it.

Harrisonburg's data center is not a proposal. The 13-acre Cyber Integration Center has been running for more than a decade; Washington, D.C.-based DBT-DATA bought it in October 2013 as its fifth data center, alongside four in Ashburn, Virginia Business reported at the time. The company said it was then the only data center in Maryland and Virginia with a Tier III certification from the Uptime Institute, and it carried LEED Silver certification. DBT Development's president, David Tolson, pitched it at federal government and private sector demand for data storage around Washington. It is a colocation building of the older kind, not a hyperscale AI campus.

What Harrisonburg has done is shut the door to the new kind arriving without a public hearing. In January 2025 the city council changed its zoning so that data centers can be built only in the industrial district and only with a special use permit, which requires public hearings and a council vote; before that, they had been allowed by right in industrial and some business zones. Community development director Adam Fletcher told council that data centers bring tax revenue but also noise, the visual impact of large, monolithic buildings, and heavy demand for water and electricity. "We need to figure out what works, what we can require," said council member Laura Dent, who raised the strain data centers elsewhere in Virginia were putting on the grid. City spokesperson Michael Parks told WHSV the aim was for residents to have their say on "if they think a project fits in their community, near their neighborhood, if it's the right use of resources."

The rest of the Shenandoah Valley is now doing the same, mostly before any developer arrives. Shenandoah County's supervisors voted 6-0 in June 2026 to require a special use permit for data centers, with rules on water, noise, setbacks and environmental impact, and rejected residents' calls for a moratorium. "Other counties have been overrun with them," said supervisor Steve Baker. Augusta County, to the south, was drafting an ordinance for a public hearing this summer; its administrator, Timothy Fitzgerald, said "the key here is to try to get out in front of any kind of major push." Further north, Frederick County has applications for the 72-acre Winchester Gateway campus and the 220-acre Virginia Technology Park near Interstate 81, and its planning commission unanimously recommended denying the Technology Park rezoning in June. The Shenandoah Valley Partnership, the regional economic development group, withdrew a grant application to find data center sites after consultants told it most developer interest in the valley had not got beyond feasibility studies.
/data-centers/united-states/virginia/har.unconfirmed: A search summary said Harrisonburg's council had voted unanimously to develop a moratorium policy by December 2026. It came from a Sierra Club page that returned an empty response, and no news source confirming it was found, so it is not reported. Directory listings in search results gave the facility's street address and building size; they were not opened and are not used. Whether the council's 2025 zoning change was final at the mid-January meeting or at the January 28 meeting WHSV mentions is not clear. No figure for the DBT facility's power draw was found in an opened source. Searches used for this page: 5.

paragraphs: Norfolk has one small data center and no fight over it, while nearby Hampton Roads cities move to restrict new ones. EdgeConneX runs a data center in part of a 100,000-square-foot building at 3800 Village Avenue, near the I-264 and I-64 interchange, occupying about 20,000 square feet with a Cox Communications data center across the street. It draws power from Dominion Energy and connects to subsea cable landings about 23 miles away in Virginia Beach.

Norfolk has not taken a side in a regional fight over what comes next. By July 2026 it had not announced a direction, while Suffolk, Chesapeake and Virginia Beach each restricted new data centers, WTKR and WHRO reported. Chesapeake council member Amanda Newins asked the state attorney general whether cities can ban data centers outright: "If the law gives us a path to say 'no', I think we all should know about it," she said.

A facility like EdgeConneX's, a colocation building serving local networks, is what Virginia Beach says it wants to protect even as it blocks large new campuses. Norfolk has not said whether it will define data centers in its zoning, require a permit, or follow its neighbors with a pause.

NTT Global Data Centers plans one of Europe's largest data centers in Nierstein, a wine town in Rheinhessen south of Frankfurt: a campus of nine buildings using about 482 megawatts of power on the Rhein-Selz-Park, the former US Army Anderson Barracks at Dexheim. Nierstein's council approved the development plan unanimously on December 10, 2025, and it took effect on January 28, 2026. In February NTT said it would file its building application in the spring and expected a permit about a year later, with construction from 2027 and the first building running in 2029.

Almost nobody has objected. Nierstein's council and the Schwabsburg village council voted unanimously to put the plans on public display, and Mayor Jochen Schmitt said there had been broad support and no opposition, only interested questions. "That doesn't happen at every site," NTT spokesman Günter Eggers said. NTT says the campus will employ about 400 people and run for at least 50 years.

NTT says the power will come entirely from renewable sources, bought mostly through contracts with German suppliers, plus solar panels and a wind farm planned on the site. Cooling is to run in a closed loop, and the town and the Rhein-Selz community want to use the waste heat. The whole campus is due to be finished around 2037.

Bavaria's main data center fight is in Wenzenbach, northeast of Regensburg. On June 5, 2026, a landowner and the Spanish energy developer IGNIS presented the town with a plan for a data center of up to 300 megawatts of power and a 100-megawatt battery plant at the Abbachhof, a medieval farm estate, an investment that could top €2 billion. The site sits beside about 21 hectares where the grid operator TenneT plans a large substation, expected by 2032.

Opposition formed within weeks. The farm's tenants were appalled, a citizens' initiative was founded, a petition against the project neared its 3,000-signature goal and the Bund Naturschutz came out against it, Regensburg Digital reported. The Abbachhof has a chapel nearly a thousand years old, and heritage officials called a demolition permit "hopeless"; the town's drinking water well is 900 meters away. On June 23 the town council passed a resolution of "constructive acknowledgement," but the town says "the council has neither approved a data center nor created building rights."

What happens next depends on the grid. TenneT is choosing which projects get power at the new substation through a review of each project's finances, land and readiness; applications ran from April to June 2026. Only if IGNIS wins a connection would the council have to decide whether to start a development plan, which it can stop at any time.

Around Munich, the established data centers belong to operators such as Equinix, which runs MU1, MU3 and MU4, the last in Aschheim east of the city; its contractor topped out a further phase, MU4.3, in July 2026.

Hamburg's data centers are small sites serving the city's internet and phone networks, and the biggest one being built is IPHH4. Portus Data Centers is building it on the Internet Port Hamburg campus on Wendenstrasse in the east of the city: two buildings of 6.4 megawatts of computer power each, with the first phase due to be finished in the last quarter of 2026, according to Data Center Dynamics. Equinix also runs a data center in the city.

The city has little power left to offer. In May 2026 the city government confirmed that Hamburg's medium- and high-voltage grid has no free connection reserves. Between 2020 and 2025 it received 110 requests for connections totaling about 4,800 megawatts, and it could not say which could be connected soon. From the second half of 2026, the city's grid company will share out spare capacity for new large connections among applicants instead of serving them first come, first served, so data centers may get waits or less power than they asked for.

Just outside the city, in Rellingen, the Hamburg cloud company X-Ion is spending nearly €80 million on DataR, a data center of up to 5 megawatts that was due to open in summer 2026. Its waste heat is to warm the neighboring Erich-Kästner-Schule and its sports hall through a local heating pilot.

Galicia's one large data center project is Galicia Green Data Center, planned on four plots totaling about 40,155 square meters in the Curtis-Teixeiro industrial estate in Curtis, A Coruña. It would be one building with three halls, up to 15 megawatts of computing capacity and its own electrical substation, at a cost of just over €50 million. The developer, Ingenostrum, now Nostrum Group and recently bought by the Australian company Iren, has pushed the opening from 2026 to 2027, eldiario.es reported in August 2026.

The regional government, the Xunta de Galicia, is a partner through Impulsa Galicia, a public-private company, and on September 9, 2024 declared the project strategic, which gives it priority and faster planning, environmental and industry approvals. It went out for public comment in January 2025. The Xunta expects about 130 construction jobs and 45 permanent ones, and pitches it as the first large facility to keep Galician companies' and institutions' data in Galicia.

The objection raised so far is to that fast track, not to the site. Greenpeace's Galicia spokesman, Manu Santos, told eldiario.es that the Xunta approves strategic projects on economic grounds without public participation: "Es la Xunta quien decide si es o no de interés para Galicia y dónde se va a emplazar y solo después la ciudadanía puede discutirlo" (the Xunta decides whether it is of interest to Galicia and where it goes, and only afterward can citizens discuss it).

North Brabant has one data center mapped: Keppel DC REIT's Eindhoven Campus, two buildings at Dillenburgstraat 25 in the De Hurk business park. The Singapore-based property trust bought it in September 2021 for €37.2 million; it has about 7,790 square meters (83,841 square feet) of rentable space, fully leased to an unnamed IT services company. A consultant quoted by Data Center Knowledge in September 2026 named Eindhoven's technology cluster as a possible place for data centers pushed out of Amsterdam.

Power is the obstacle. On September 17, 2026, grid operator Enexis put more than 85,000 planned new homes in its area on a waiting list because the grid has no room, and the squeeze is worst in Brabant, especially the east of the province. Any large new data center here would compete for the same scarce capacity. TenneT is due to publish in December 2026 how much capacity is available in each area, released step by step from early 2027.

Two data center campuses are growing in Carnaxide, in Oeiras, close to where undersea internet cables land at Carcavelos. AtlasEdge opened its LIS001 building there on October 28, 2025, the first stage of a campus it says will cost more than €500 million and reach 30 megawatts of power. Digital Realty bought a building and land in Carnaxide for $8.3 million and expects it to open in early 2027 with up to 2.4 megawatts. In Vila Franca de Xira, Merlin Properties is building a 36-megawatt data center.

The strain is on the power grid. According to the environmental group ZERO, data centers account for more than 70% of the capacity requested from grid operator REN. A 2026 government resolution treats data centers as critical infrastructure and speeds up approvals; ZERO says it sets no binding rules on renewable power, water or waste heat, and warns data centers risk becoming "predators of resources" (translated from Portuguese). Renewable energy developer João Correia asked who will pay for the grid upgrades they need, if not ordinary consumers through their bills.

Lazio's biggest data center plan is at Colleferro, in the province of Rome, where on August 11, 2026, the town council approved an AI data center by Cobra Green Hyperscale on 76 hectares between the A1 motorway, the Via Casilina and the high-speed railway. It has 150 megawatts of grid power assigned by the national grid operator Terna, a 34-megawatt solar plant and a closed-loop cooling system meant to limit water use. It still needs a single permit from the Ministry of Environment and Energy Security, under a new procedure that takes up to ten months.

At Santa Palomba in Pomezia, Rai Way, the infrastructure arm of the state broadcaster Rai, presented a 35.2-megawatt data center on March 17, 2026, after getting its building permit. It replaces Rai's medium-wave transmitter, in service since 1929, and cranes began taking down one of the giant masts in September. Construction would take 24 to 30 months once customers sign, possibly starting before 2027, and Rai Way must give the town land for an access road. Pomezia's mayor, Veronica Felici, said the town had worked for years to make it happen.

Inside Rome, Aruba's €300 million Hyper Cloud campus at the Tecnopolo Tiburtino is planned for five data centers and 30 megawatts, with the first building running since October 2024. No date has been set for the ministry's decision on Colleferro.

Piedmont's old car and printing plants are being offered to the world as data center land, and the numbers requested from the grid are far larger than anything yet built. As of July 31, 2026, according to the national grid operator Terna's data reported by the Turin paper La Voce, there were 64 data center connection requests in Piedmont totalling 13.13 gigawatts, 43 of them in the metropolitan city of Turin for 8.08 gigawatts. A connection request is not a data center; many may be speculative, and the paper said the gigawatts had not yet been matched to named companies, addresses and projects.

Some of them have. At Grugliasco, on the former Pininfarina site in Borgata Lesna, a first module of about 58,000 square metres is described at around 200 megawatts and €4 billion, with at least 200 jobs promised; the end user has not been named, and the town council voted on June 30, 2026, with 17 in favour, to recognise a public interest in the planning exemption it needs. Requests at Grugliasco total 1.23 gigawatts. In Turin itself, Reba Projects, linked to Agostino Re Rebaudengo's Asja group, plans a data center at the former Bonafous rolling mill in Lucento, starting at 125 megawatts and possibly exceeding 300, for more than €1 billion; the Region has authorised two 220-kilovolt underground lines to it, and Iren has designed a network to carry its waste heat. At Caselle, near the airport, Hines is developing six buildings of more than 150,000 square metres with a 250-megawatt connection on land rezoned from a shopping centre scheme. In Moncalieri, the former ILTE printing works in Vadò is the site of a four-building campus plan, and Settimo Torinese's mayor Elena Piastra says she has received eight requests for data centers. The largest single project is outside the Turin area, at the former Galileo Ferraris power station at Trino in the province of Vercelli: TechBau's Cavour Hyperscale Campus, around €4 billion, which the national cabinet declared of pre-eminent national strategic interest, with a government commissioner to speed its single authorisation, expected in 2027, and first operation in 2028.

The objections so far are about what is not known. La Voce argued that before any planning exemption a council should know at least who is coming, the real power draw, the cooling system and water need, noise, emergency generators and how many workers will remain after construction, and noted that a data center can draw hundreds of megawatts without needing thousands of workers at the gates. The activist site infoaut calls it a "barbarian invasion" and warns of pressure on farmland from the solar and battery plants needed to power it. A regional councillor for AVS, Valentina Cera, has pressed the Region to speed up its data center law in light of the Moncalieri plan.

The Region is now drafting that law. It has held a public consultation and, environment councillor Matteo Marnati said on September 22, 2026, the submissions are being examined by its technical offices. The draft treats data centers as more than technology sheds: it would classify land into zones of attraction, repulsion and exclusion, and set a minimum share of renewable power, limits on emergency generators, low-water cooling, waste heat recovery and efficiency thresholds. When the bill goes to the regional council, and whether it will apply to projects already in the pipeline, has not been announced.
/data-centers/italy/piedmont/.unconfirmed: The Grugliasco council vote date and vote count come from infoaut, an activist site, which cites La Voce and La Repubblica Torino; La Voce's opened text does not give them. infoaut also gives Moncalieri as 576MW and €4.5 billion, attributed to La Repubblica Torino, which was not opened, so those figures are not used; La Voce gives about 600MW of requests there. The Trino press release date could not be fixed from the page; the cabinet decision is from 2026. A May 2026 question in Turin's city council about planned data centers was seen only in search results and is not reported. This site's map lists an Oracle cloud region in Turin; no opened source reported on it. Quotes and terms translated from Italian. Searches used for this page: 1.

paragraphs: Anhui's data centers are concentrated in one city chosen by Beijing. In 2022 the national "East Data, West Computing" programme set up a network of eight hubs and ten data center clusters, and Wuhu, Anhui's second-largest city, became one of the two clusters of the Yangtze River Delta hub, meant to supply computing to Shanghai, Jiangsu and Zhejiang. Wuhu's pitch, repeated in its local media, is fibre latency of about 5 milliseconds to Shanghai and Hangzhou and 2 to Nanjing, cheaper land and power than the coast, and Anhui's position as the only Yangtze River Delta province with a net surplus of electricity. The city has set itself the goal of becoming a "computing power center city"; the core of the cluster's starting zone is a development called China Digital Island.

Huawei is the anchor. Its Huawei Cloud East China (Wuhu) data center on China Digital Island was already operating in 2025, when Huawei deployed its CloudMatrix 384 supernodes there at scale, and a Huawei executive, Yu Chengdong, said it would supply computing for the company's intelligent vehicle research. In September 2026 Huawei unveiled in Wuhu a four-storey "3D data center" that stacks cooling, computing, power and backup power vertically, which it says can host Ascend supernode clusters of more than 100,000 accelerator cards. Huawei says more than 90 percent of the mechanical and electrical systems can be prefabricated and that the Wuhu facility took about nine months to build against 18 to 24 months for a conventional build, and that its cloud business is deploying the design at its core hubs in Gui'an, Inner Mongolia and Wuhu. "We treat the data center as a standard product that can be replicated at scale, rather than a bespoke engineering project," said Huawei senior vice president Ren Shulu. The state telecom carriers are here too: China Telecom opened its only group-level cloud computing center in Anhui in Wuhu in 2017, and China Telecom, China Mobile and China Unicom all have computing centers connected to the Wuhu cluster's platform.

The scale is described in the state's own units. By September 2025 the Wuhu cluster platform connected 34 data centers with nearly 640 petaflops of general computing, nearly 26,000 petaflops of AI computing, 33.3 petaflops of supercomputing and 2,070 qubits of quantum computing, and Wuhu held 70 percent of Anhui's AI computing capacity, according to a WeChat analysis republished by 36Kr; a Wuhu government release, undated, reports 28 more data centers added to what is now also the Anhui provincial scheduling platform, now linked with those of five other central provinces. The largest users named are iFlytek, NIO and Zhixiang Future. No figure for the cluster's electricity or water use has been published, and no local opposition to any Anhui data center has been reported.

The doubts on record are commercial. The Wuhu government itself, in a report quoted by 36Kr, acknowledged "a certain gap in terms of talent resources, industrial foundation, and technological innovation" and that "the electricity price is higher compared with the western hubs." Researchers cited in the same piece pointed to poor matching of supply and demand, with computing utilisation in Hefei at only 65 percent. Competing Yangtze River Delta clusters are targeting similar capacity, 60,000 petaflops of AI computing by 2027 in the integrated demonstration zone alone. An Anhui provincial decision on the digital economy that took effect on October 1, 2025 commits the province to accelerating the Wuhu cluster further.
/data-centers/china/anhui/.unconfirmed: Computing figures in petaflops (P) and qubits are official Chinese metrics as relayed by 36Kr from a WeChat account ('Urban Evolution Theory'); they are not power figures and cannot be converted to megawatts. The Wuhu government release on 28 new data centers is undated in the extracted text. This site's map lists two Huawei Wuhu sites (Jiangbei and Sanshan); the opened sources name only a Huawei Cloud East China (Wuhu) data center on China Digital Island, so which of the two it is was not established. The 3D data center's power rating appeared only in a search-result headline and is not used. Searches used for this page: 2.

paragraphs: Henan's data centers are concentrated in the Zhengzhou Airport Economy Zone, a national-level development zone beside Zhengzhou's international airport that also hosts Foxconn and a BYD car plant. The newest is a national AI computing center: on April 14, 2026, what state television called China's largest scientific AI computing cluster began operating at the national supercomputing network's core node in Zhengzhou, built on Chinese-made chips. A separate large AI computing cluster in Zhengzhou opened its first phase in 2025 and is planned to become the biggest in central China.

The state phone carriers and the server maker Inspur have built near the airport for more than a decade. In 2015 Inspur started a 3 billion yuan Yunhai science and technology park there, which it called the largest cloud data center ever built in Henan, cooled by outside air for 38% of the year.

In October 2021 China Telecom broke ground on its 3.4 billion yuan Central China data center in the airport district, a key provincial project. Its first phase, two data halls and a generator building, was scheduled for delivery in June 2022; no news of its completion has been published.

Shandong's contribution to China's data center build-out is as much about the equipment that powers them as the buildings themselves. The server maker Inspur has built on a large scale in Jinan: the first phase of its Jinan data center, brought into use in 2014, had 216,000 square metres of floor space, 3,800 racks and 120,000 servers, and the company said the complete facility could accommodate up to 304,000 racks and a million servers, Data Center Dynamics reported. Inspur also built a ¥3.1 billion national key laboratory for high-performance servers and storage and an integrated circuit park in the province.

The newest development is in Qingdao. On June 6, 2026, the Qingdao power equipment maker TGOOD Electric began operating what state media called the world's first prefabricated power hub built for AI data centers, which it calls the "AI PowerHouse." It is a cluster of factory-built modules about 53 by 41 metres, covering some 2,200 square metres, that integrates high-voltage and solid-state transformers and gas-insulated switchgear, connects to the 110- or 220-kilovolt grid, and delivers 800-volt direct current to AI servers. CCTV, as reported by the South China Morning Post, said it allows direct connection to renewable power with "100 per cent green electricity consumption" TGOOD makes further claims for its speed, cost and land use. "We ensure every device can access three different power supplies," said TGOOD executive president Zhou Jun. It was already connected to a privately operated data center and was expected to be adopted by national-level computing facilities in the second half of 2026.

Those performance figures come from the developer and state outlets and have not been independently verified, as the tech news site Let's Data Science noted; the hub's capacity in megawatts was not disclosed. No figure for Shandong's total data center electricity or water use, and no public objection to any Shandong data center, has been publicly reported. This site maps a Huawei Cloud site in Qingdao, but no opened source reported on it.
/data-centers/china/shandong/.unconfirmed: The Inspur Jinan figures are from DCD stories of 2012 and 2015; whether the Jinan complex reached its planned 304,000 racks was not found. The June 6 opening date is from CCTV via SCMP ('Saturday', June 7 story); ECNS also says Saturday. The 800V DC and grid-voltage details are Xinhua's as relayed by Let's Data Science. paragraphs: Fujian's main data center district is the Digital Fujian (Changle) Industrial Park, also called the Southeast Big Data Industrial Park, in the Binhai New City area of Fuzhou, the provincial capital. The provincial, city and Changle governments have planned it together since 2013. The province lists the Digital Fujian Cloud Computing Center, Qihoo 360 and Inspur among its main big data tenants, and China Daily reported in 2019 that more than 130 companies, including Microsoft and Tencent, had moved in.

The province's newer push is AI computing on Chinese hardware. At a Fuzhou conference on December 19, 2025, Newland Hi-Tech Group signed an agreement with Huawei to build services around Huawei's Ascend AI chips, the Fuzhou Daily reported. In Xiamen, Xiamen Torch Group won a roughly 51,150-square-meter plot in May 2022, west of West Binhai Avenue and north of Meifeng Ecological Park, for the Xiamen Digital Industrial Computing Center, a supercomputing center meant to serve factories in Xiamen Science City and Tongxiang High-tech City.
